help.title: User guide
body: The simulator has two linked, time-synchronised views — the **Horizon diagram** (what you see) and the **Celestial sphere** (why the sky moves that way) — and four groups of controls below them.
## Review and Present
- **Review:** 12 short scored tasks with hints and explanations (key **L**).
- **Present:** full screen, large text and hidden control panels for projecting to an audience (key **F**; press **F** or **Esc** to leave).
## The two views
### Celestial sphere
An Earth-centred model, with a white dot marking the observer's location.
- {{#4f9dff}} **Celestial polar axis** — blue.
- {{#ffd54f}} **Celestial equator** — yellow.
- {{#a3a3a3}} **0h hour circle** — grey.
- The sky is simulated as turning, apparently, about the celestial polar axis.
### Horizon diagram
The sky as seen by an observer at the centre of the horizon plane. Directions are marked:
**N** — north · **E** — east · **S** — south · **W** — west
### Interaction
- **Drag:** rotate the view.
- **Scroll or pinch:** zoom in or out.
- **Click a star:** open its details.
- **Hover over a line:** see what it is.
- **Observer's view:** move the camera to the observer's position and look at the sky as you would outdoors.
## Control panels
On wide screens in Full mode the panels and data bar are collapsed to give the horizon diagram more room: press **Control panels** or **Data** below the views to open them.
### 01 · Observer location
Set the observer's geographic position in any of these ways:
- Type the latitude and longitude.
- Move the latitude slider.
- Pick a point on the map.
- Choose one of the preset sites in Vietnam.
- Explore the special cases: the equator and the two poles.
### 02 · Animation & time
Control the apparent motion of the sky:
- Play or pause the simulation.
- Choose continuous, one sidereal day, or hour-by-hour playback.
- Adjust the rate.
- Drag the **sidereal time** slider to turn the sky by hand.
### 03 · Display
Choose what is drawn:
- Coordinate lines and reference planes.
- The circumpolar, rising-and-setting and never-rising zones.
- Angles and arcs for studying the geometry of the celestial sphere.
- Labels for each group of objects.
- Extra layers: the ecliptic, the Sun and the Milky Way.
### 04 · Stars
Study and build different star fields:
- Add constellation figures.
- Generate random stars.
- Create a star from its coordinates \((\alpha, \delta)\).
- Show the catalogue of real bright stars.
- Set the length of star trails to follow apparent motion over time.
## Basic relations and formulae
The simulator uses the standard relations of spherical astronomy to find apparent positions.
$$ Local sidereal time :: \mathrm{LST} = \mathrm{GST} + \lambda
$$ Hour angle :: H = \mathrm{LST} - \alpha
$$ Altitude :: \sin h = \sin\varphi\,\sin\delta + \cos\varphi\,\cos\delta\,\cos H
$$ Azimuth (from north, increasing eastwards) :: A = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-\cos\delta\,\sin H,\; \sin\delta\,\cos\varphi - \cos\delta\,\cos H\,\sin\varphi\right)
### Some key geometric relations
$$ Altitude of the celestial pole :: h_P = |\varphi|
$$ Angle between celestial equator and horizon :: \theta = 90^\circ - |\varphi|
$$ Northern Hemisphere — circumpolar when :: \delta > 90^\circ - \varphi
$$ Northern Hemisphere — never rises when :: \delta < -\left(90^\circ - \varphi\right)
In the **Southern Hemisphere** these conditions are mirrored across the celestial equator.
### Rising and setting
$$ Hour angle at rising or setting :: \cos H_0 = -\tan\varphi\,\tan\delta
$$ Time spent above the horizon :: T = \dfrac{2H_0}{15}
with \(T\) in sidereal hours and \(H_0\) in degrees.
## Keyboard shortcuts
|| Key | Action
| Space | Play or pause the simulation
| ← → | Go back or forward 1 sidereal hour
| + − | Speed up or slow down
| N | Set the time to now
| V | Reset star trails
| C | Restore the default view
| L | Open or close Review
| F | Turn presentation mode (full screen) on or off
| H | Open this guide
| Esc | Close a dialog or Review; otherwise clear the selection

about.title: About
body: **AstroSphere – Celestial Coordinate System Simulator**

AstroSphere is a celestial coordinate system simulator developed by the **STEM & Experiential Learning in Astronomy Research Group – USAC Astronomy Club**, with the aim of providing an intuitive educational tool for teaching, learning, and independent study of fundamental astronomy.

The system is designed to help students progressively develop an intuitive understanding of **celestial sphere geometry, the apparent motion of the sky, and astronomical coordinate systems**. By visually demonstrating the relationship between the altitude of the celestial pole and geographic latitude, as well as the transformations between the equatorial coordinate system \((\alpha, \delta, H)\) and the horizontal coordinate system \((A, h)\), AstroSphere enables learners to observe and understand fundamental astronomical phenomena, including the rising and setting of celestial objects, circumpolar stars that never fall below the horizon, and the distinctive position of Polaris in the night sky.
## Methodology & Accuracy
- Sidereal time calculations follow the IAU 1982 conventions. Coordinate transformations are automatically validated against the astronomy-engine library, with an error of less than \(0.1^\circ\).
- Celestial coordinates are referenced to the J2000.0 epoch. The current version does not yet account for proper motion, precession, nutation, or atmospheric refraction.
- The Earth–celestial sphere model is significantly exaggerated relative to its actual scale to emphasize the geometric relationships between the observer, the horizon, and the celestial sphere.
## Data Sources & Technology
- **Star Catalogue & Constellation Lines:** Based on d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn, released under the BSD-3-Clause License. The underlying stellar data are derived from the HYG Database.
- **Geographic Maps:** Natural Earth (public domain), distributed through the world-atlas package.

- **Stellar Distances (Fly Through Space Mode):** Based on Hipparcos trigonometric parallaxes, New Reduction (van Leeuwen, 2007; Catalogue I/311), accessed through the VizieR service of CDS Strasbourg.

- **Exoplanets:** NASA Exoplanet Archive, using the Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table. This research has made use of the NASA Exoplanet Archive, operated by the California Institute of Technology under contract with NASA as part of the Exoplanet Exploration Program.

- **Planetary Positions & Physical Properties:** Based on approximate JPL orbital elements (Standish), NASA NSSDCA planetary fact sheets, and rotational axis orientation data from the IAU Working Group on Cartographic Coordinates and Rotational Elements (WGCCRE, 2015). Lunar positions are calculated using Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, Chapter 47.

- **Vietnamese Constellation Names:** Sourced from the Vietnamese Wikipedia article Danh sách chòm sao (List of Constellations), licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. On the celestial map, stars and constellations are identified using their internationally recognized IAU designations, while Vietnamese names are provided in the detailed information panels.
- **3D Graphics:** Three.js, released under the MIT License.
- **Mathematical Rendering:** KaTeX, released under the MIT License.

- **Academic References & Design:** The system draws on the visualization approaches of educational astronomy simulation tools, such as the Rotating Sky Explorer developed by the Nebraska Astronomy Applet Project (NAAP) at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln. All source code, interfaces, and system assets have been independently developed by USAC.
## System Architecture

AstroSphere follows an **offline-first** design philosophy, allowing the system to operate entirely within a web browser without requiring an internet connection once all necessary resources have been downloaded.

catalog.title: Reference catalogue of celestial objects
intro: Designations follow international standards (**Messier**, **NGC/IC** and **PGC** catalogues; **IAU/MPC** comet designations) so they can be looked up consistently in SIMBAD, NED and VizieR. Click a designation to open its SIMBAD page (requires a network connection).
Coordinates refer to the J2000.0 epoch. Distances are rounded reference values; for remote galaxies the uncertainty can reach 10–20 %.
catalog.dsoTitle: Notable galaxies, nebulae and star clusters
catalog.dsoNote: The table lists notable objects only. Turn on “Deep-sky objects” under Display → Extras to see all {n} objects on the sky; click one to see its data.
sources: **Symbols:** \(q\) is the perihelion distance (astronomical units), \(e\) the eccentricity, \(i\) the orbital inclination to the ecliptic. Comets move quickly against the stars, so they are not drawn on the simulated sky.

**Sources:** coordinates, magnitudes and sizes of deep-sky objects from d3-celestial (BSD-3); reference distances from SIMBAD/NED and NASA; comet orbits from the JPL Small-Body Database and the IAU Minor Planet Center (rounded). “Fly Through Space”: stellar distances from Hipparcos parallaxes (van Leeuwen 2007, via VizieR); exoplanets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.
